name: Ghandruk
tagline: A Gurung village of stone roofs facing Annapurna South
meta_description: Ghandruk guide: Gurung stone village at about 2,000 m, Annapurna South views, the Poon Hill loop, homestays, ACAP and guide rules, jeep and trek routes from Pokhara.
summary: Ghandruk is a large Gurung village at about 2,000 m, 32 km north-west of Pokhara, with Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machapuchare filling the skyline. Reach it by jeep and short walk, or as part of the Poon Hill loop. It needs an ACAP permit and, under current rules, a licensed guide.
intro: Ghandruk spreads down a steep slope above the Modi Khola in stone terraces, its houses roofed with grey slate and joined by flagstone paths. Gurung families make up most of the village, and like many Gurung villages it sent generations of men into the British and Indian Gurkha regiments; pension money and trekking income built many of the newer lodges. In clear weather, Annapurna South (7,219 m), Hiunchuli and Machapuchare stand almost straight above the rooftops.

The village lies inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, Nepal's largest protected area at 7,629 km². It sits on the routes to Annapurna Base Camp and on the Poon Hill loop, so it is busy in October and April, with quieter weeks in between. A jeep road now reaches Kimche and nearby points, so people with limited time can get here from Pokhara in 3–4 hours and walk the last stretch.

Ghandruk is one of the best introductions to the Himalaya for families and first-time trekkers: high enough to feel the mountains, low enough at about 2,000 m that altitude is rarely a concern. Stay a night or two in a lodge or homestay, visit the Gurung museum and walk to the viewpoint above the village at dawn.

highlights.title: Annapurna South at the doorstep
highlights.text: From the upper village, Annapurna South (7,219 m), Hiunchuli (6,441 m) and Machapuchare (6,993 m) rise above the Modi Khola gorge. The best light is at dawn from October to February.

highlights.title: The Gurung cultural museum
highlights.text: A small museum in a traditional house shows Gurung tools, dress, musical instruments and household objects. Local volunteers explain how they were used. A small fee supports its upkeep.

highlights.title: Stone lanes and slate roofs
highlights.text: Walk the flagstone paths down through the older part of the village, where houses have carved wooden windows, slate roofs and courtyards drying millet and maize in autumn.

highlights.title: On the Poon Hill loop
highlights.text: Ghandruk is the last night on the classic loop from Nayapul over Ghorepani and Poon Hill (3,210 m) via Tadapani. Walking in the other direction, it is the first night.

highlights.title: Rhododendron forests
highlights.text: The trail from Ghandruk up to Tadapani climbs through forests of rhododendron, Nepal's national flower, which turn red and pink in March and April.

field_notes.fact: Ghandruk is a traditional Gurung settlement about 32 km north-west of Pokhara at roughly 2,012 m, with views of Annapurna South (7,219 m), Machapuchare (6,993 m), Gangapurna and Hiunchuli.
The Annapurna Conservation Area, which includes Ghandruk, covers 7,629 km² across five districts and is Nepal's largest protected area.
Poon Hill, the dawn viewpoint on the loop through Ghandruk, stands at 3,210 m and looks across to Annapurna I (8,091 m), Dhaulagiri, Annapurna South and Machapuchare.

local_word.meaning: new year; Tamu Lhosar, the Gurung new year, falls around late December

how_to_reach.text: Fly to Pokhara, then continue by road. Kathmandu–Pokhara flights take about 25 minutes.
Local buses and shared jeeps leave Pokhara's Baglung bus park for Nayapul and on to Kimche; the ride takes 2.5–4 hours depending on road condition. Walk up to Ghandruk in 1–1.5 hours from Kimche.
A private jeep from Pokhara reaches Kimche or the upper roadhead in about 2.5–3 hours. The road is rough and can close after heavy rain; check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Saver: Ghandruk has dozens of teahouse lodges and a community homestay programme where you sleep in a Gurung family house and eat with them; rooms run ₹300–1,000 a night and most lodges expect you to eat where you sleep. Comfort: several newer lodges in the upper village have attached bathrooms, solar hot water and mountain-facing rooms. Signature: there is no luxury lodge in Ghandruk itself; on signature trips we pair one night here with Tiger Mountain Pokhara Lodge.
tips: Get your ACAP permit in Pokhara or Kathmandu; it costs double if bought at a checkpoint.
Arrange a licensed guide through a registered agency; it is required for foreigners in the conservation area under the 2023 rule. Check current status before you travel.
Order dal bhat for refills and to keep costs down.
Carry a water filter or purification tablets; lodges sell boiled water.
Bring a warm layer; nights fall to near freezing from December to February.

experiences.title: Ghandruk's stone lanes and Gurung museum
experiences.summary: A slow walk through Ghandruk's flagstone lanes, past slate-roofed houses and terraces, with a stop at the Gurung museum to understand village life and the community's long ties to the Gurkha regiments.
body: Start from the upper village, where newer lodges face the mountains, and walk down the stone steps into the older part of Ghandruk. Houses here are built of stone with slate roofs and small carved windows. In autumn, millet and maize dry on rooftops and in courtyards, and buffaloes and goats are kept in sheds below the living rooms.

The Gurung cultural museum is set in a traditional house. It displays farm tools, bamboo baskets, weaving looms, brass pots, clothing and musical instruments, with village volunteers to explain them. The Gurung people speak their own Tibeto-Burman language, Tamu Kyi, and celebrate Tamu Lhosar, their new year, around late December.

Many Ghandruk families have relatives in the Gurkha regiments of the British and Indian armies, and some houses show photos of soldiers in uniform. Walk respectfully, ask before photographing people, and buy tea or snacks in village shops to support local families.

faqs.q: What language do Gurung people speak?
faqs.a: Gurung, also called Tamu Kyi, a Tibeto-Burman language. Nearly everyone in Ghandruk also speaks Nepali, and lodge owners speak some English and Hindi.

faqs.q: Is the Ghandruk museum open every day?
faqs.a: Usually, but hours depend on volunteers. Ask at your lodge in the morning.

faqs.q: Can I visit a Gurung family home?
faqs.a: Yes, through the homestay programme or by invitation. Remove shoes, accept tea with both hands and ask before taking photos.

experiences.title: Poon Hill dawn on the Ghandruk loop
experiences.cost: ₹3,000–4,500 a day including shared guide, lodge and food
experiences.summary: The classic short trek of Nepal: up through Ulleri to Ghorepani, sunrise from Poon Hill at 3,210 m, then across forested ridges to Tadapani and down to Ghandruk. Four or five days, teahouses every night and views of Dhaulagiri and the Annapurnas.
body: Most people start by jeep from Pokhara to Nayapul or further up to Tikhedhunga or Ulleri, then climb the long stone staircase to Ulleri (about 2,000 m) and on through rhododendron and oak forest to Ghorepani (about 2,860 m). Ghorepani is a cluster of lodges on a saddle, busy in season, with views of Dhaulagiri and Annapurna South from its upper streets.

Wake at about 4:30 am and climb for 45–60 minutes to Poon Hill at 3,210 m. As the sun rises, the panorama lights from Dhaulagiri (8,167 m) and its icefall across to Annapurna I, Annapurna South, Hiunchuli and Machapuchare. After breakfast in Ghorepani, walk east over a forested ridge to Deurali and down to Tadapani (about 2,600 m), then the next day down to Ghandruk.

The trek is moderate, with long stone staircases, but the highest sleeping point is under 3,000 m, so altitude problems are rare. You need an ACAP permit and, for foreigners under the 2023 rule, a licensed guide; check current status before you travel. From Ghandruk, a jeep takes you back to Pokhara.

faqs.q: How hard is the Poon Hill trek?
faqs.a: Moderate. Expect 5–7 hours of walking a day, with long stone staircases. Anyone reasonably fit can do it. The highest point is 3,210 m, at the viewpoint.

faqs.q: How many days is the Poon Hill and Ghandruk trek?
faqs.a: Four days from Pokhara is common if you take jeeps at both ends; five is more relaxed.

faqs.q: Can Indians do the Poon Hill trek without a guide?
faqs.a: The 2023 rule requires foreign trekkers in conservation areas to use a licensed guide, and checkposts may apply it to Indians. Plan for a guide. Check current status before you travel.

experiences.title: Dinner and a night in a Gurung homestay
experiences.cost: ₹1,200–2,500 per person with dinner and breakfast
experiences.summary: Stay with a Gurung family in Ghandruk's homestay programme, eat dal bhat with seasonal vegetables and pickles cooked on a wood or gas stove, and learn how a hill farm works from the people who run it.
body: Ghandruk has a community-run homestay programme where visitors stay in family houses rather than lodges. Rooms are simple, often with shared bathrooms, but clean. You eat with the family or in their kitchen, which is usually the warmest room in the house. Book through your guide or the village homestay office.

Dinner is usually dal bhat: rice or millet, lentils, a vegetable curry, greens from the garden, and achar, a fresh or fermented pickle. In season you may get buckwheat or millet bread, local honey and buffalo or goat curd. Gurung families also make local alcohol from millet; it is offered, never required.

Ask about farming, the year's festivals and family members working abroad or in the army. Children in the house may practise their English with you. In the morning, join the family for tea on the terrace as the mountains come out. Homestay income stays in the village.

faqs.q: How do I book a homestay in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Through your trekking agency or guide, or at the village homestay counter. Pay the family directly or through the programme, as advised.
Dal bhat is vegetarian, and families are used to vegetarian guests. Tell them in advance if you do not eat eggs or meat.
Some do; many share a bathroom. Hot water is usually solar or gas and may be limited in the evening.

faqs.q: How do I reach Ghandruk from Pokhara?
faqs.a: Take a shared jeep or bus from Pokhara's Baglung bus park towards Nayapul and on to Kimche, about 2.5–4 hours, then walk up to Ghandruk in 1–1.5 hours. A private jeep is faster. Or walk in as part of the Poon Hill loop.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Yes, the ACAP permit, because Ghandruk is inside the Annapurna Conservation Area. In 2026 it costs NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals and NPR 3,000 for others, and double at checkpoints. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Ghandruk suitable for kids and seniors?
faqs.a: Yes, with care. The jeep road reduces walking to 1–1.5 hours, the altitude of about 2,000 m rarely causes problems, and lodges are comfortable. The stone steps are steep, so take it slowly.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and wifi in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Yes, Nepal Telecom and Ncell work in most of the village, and most lodges have wifi, which can be slow in the evening.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ghandruk?
faqs.a: October and November give the clearest views. March and April bring rhododendron flowers. December to February is cold but often clear. June to September is wet with leeches and cloud.

faqs.q: How much does a night in Ghandruk cost?
faqs.a: A lodge or homestay room costs ₹300–1,000, and dal bhat ₹400–650. With breakfast, dinner, tea and snacks, budget ₹1,800–2,800 per person per day, excluding a guide.

faqs.q: Can I see Annapurna from Ghandruk?
faqs.a: Yes, Annapurna South (7,219 m), Hiunchuli and Machapuchare are directly visible. Annapurna I is hidden behind; you see it from Poon Hill.

faqs.q: Is altitude sickness a risk in Ghandruk?
faqs.a: At about 2,000 m, it is unlikely for healthy travellers. On the Poon Hill loop the highest sleeping point is Ghorepani at about 2,860 m. If you have heart or lung conditions, talk to your doctor.
Do not rely on one. Carry enough cash from Pokhara for lodges, food, permits and tips.
